overview:
Guatemala lies just south of Mexico in Central America, bordered by Belize, Honduras and El Salvador, with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. It covers about 109,000 km², roughly the size of the US state of Tennessee, and with about 18 million people it is the most populous country in Central America. Guatemala City, the capital, is the region's largest city.

Nearly half of Guatemalans are Maya, descendants of the civilization that built great stone cities in the jungle more than a thousand years ago. Spanish is the official language, but 22 Mayan languages such as K'iche', Q'eqchi' and Kaqchikel are spoken daily, along with Garifuna and Xinca. Women in highland villages wear hand-woven blouses called huipiles whose patterns reveal their hometown.

Guatemala is a republic with an elected president. Coffee, bananas, sugar and textiles are major products, and many Guatemalans work abroad and send money home. Volcanoes, colonial towns, colorful markets and the ruins of Tikal draw visitors from around the world.
landAndNature:
A ridge of about 37 volcanoes runs across southern Guatemala, several of them active. Fuego throws out ash and lava regularly, Pacaya lets hikers roast marshmallows over hot rocks, and Tajumulco, about 4,220 meters, is the highest peak in Central America. Lake Atitlán, ringed by three volcanoes and Maya villages, is often called the most beautiful lake in the world.

The north is the flat, forested Petén lowland, where the ruins of Tikal poke above the jungle canopy and spider monkeys, toucans and jaguars roam the Maya Biosphere Reserve. The Caribbean side is hot and humid; the highlands are cool and springlike, earning Guatemala the name Land of Eternal Spring. The resplendent quetzal, a brilliant green bird with tail feathers up to a meter long, is the national bird and gives its name to the currency.
peopleAndCulture:
Maya traditions are alive in Guatemala: the K'iche' epic Popol Vuh tells the story of creation, and the ancient Maya calendar is still used by spiritual leaders. The Sunday market at Chichicastenango overflows with woven textiles, masks and flowers. Ladinos, people of mixed heritage, and the Garifuna of the Caribbean coast add their own music and food.

Corn is sacred and central: tortillas come with every meal, along with black beans, tamales, and rich stews like pepián and kak'ik turkey soup. The Maya were the first people to make chocolate drinks from cacao. The marimba, a wooden xylophone, is the national instrument. During Holy Week, Antigua's streets are carpeted in colored sawdust designs, and on November 1 the towns of Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez fly enormous kites to honor the dead. Soccer is the favorite sport.
history:
The Maya civilization reached its height in Guatemala between about 250 and 900 AD, when cities such as Tikal, El Mirador and Quiriguá built towering pyramids, developed writing and tracked the planets with remarkable accuracy. Many cities were abandoned after 900, but Maya kingdoms in the highlands were still powerful when Spanish soldiers under Pedro de Alvarado invaded in 1524.

Guatemala became independent from Spain in 1821 and a separate republic in 1847. In the 1900s, coffee and banana companies, especially the US-owned United Fruit Company, held enormous power. A reform government was overthrown in a 1954 coup backed by the United States, leading to a civil war from 1960 to 1996 in which about 200,000 people, most of them Maya civilians, were killed. Peace accords in 1996 ended the fighting; four years earlier, the Maya activist Rigoberta Menchú had won the Nobel Peace Prize for defending Indigenous rights.
funFacts: Guatemala's currency, the quetzal, is named after a bird whose tail feathers the ancient Maya used as money.
Tikal's Temple IV, about 70 meters tall, appeared as a rebel base in the original Star Wars film in 1977.
The Maya used cacao beans as currency and drank chocolate spiced with chili, not sweetened with sugar.
Guatemala's name may come from a Nahuatl word meaning "place of many trees."
On the Day of the Dead, kite makers in Sumpango fly circular kites up to 20 meters across.
Antigua Guatemala was the colonial capital until earthquakes in 1773 destroyed much of it, prompting a move to the present capital.
